text: Show why K, the length of the shortest program producing a string, cannot be computed. Fill in the three blanks.
choices: // Suppose K were computable. Write a program that, given n, searches strings
// in order and returns the first with ___ .
// Such a string exists (most strings of length n+1 qualify), so the search ends.
// But that program's own length is about ___ bits,
// and it outputs a string whose complexity exceeds n. So n < K(s) <= that length.
// This is false for large n, because ___ . Contradiction.
answer: K(s) > n|c + log2(n)|c + log2(n) grows more slowly than n
explanation: It is the Berry paradox made rigorous — "the smallest number not describable in fewer than twelve words" is a description of it in eleven — and Chaitin turned that wordplay into a theorem. Note the shape: a short description producing something which by assumption has no short description, exactly as `trouble` was a program contradicting its own prediction.
